name: Eytzinger-layout keyword search
listed_description: Binary search over keywords stored in breadth-first (Eytzinger) order instead of sorted order, to improve cache locality of the lexer keyword filter.
claim_text: Changing memory layout to Eytzinger order increases cache locality and therefore speeds up the search (qualitative, no numbers).
guessed_baseline: std::lower_bound binary search on sorted array
found_in: book: Learn LLVM 17, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 8, Generating C++ code from a TableGen file

name: Czech-Havas-Majewski minimal perfect hash generation (keyword filter)
listed_description: Classic graph-based algorithm for generating minimal perfect hash functions, proposed in the book as a way to build a generated token filter that beats llvm::StringMap.
claim_text: Easily implemented and gives very good performance; a generated perfect-hash token filter is a candidate to be faster than llvm::StringMap (no numbers).
found_in: book: Learn LLVM 17, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 8, Performance of the token filter

name: TableGen-generated token filter (tinylang keyword lookup)
listed_description: Custom TableGen backend that generates a keyword lookup function (TokenFilter.inc) from the token database, replacing the llvm::StringMap based keyword filter.
listed_license: MIT (companion repository, per its GitHub page)
claim_text: A plain binary search does not beat the llvm::StringMap implementation; a generated perfect hash function is needed to beat it.
book_benchmark: No timings given. Book only states that generated binary search gave no gain over llvm::StringMap and suggests perfect hashing as next step.
found_in: book: Learn LLVM 17, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 8, Generating C++ code from a TableGen file / Performance of the token filter

name: libFuzzer
listed_description: In-process, coverage-guided fuzz testing library shipped in LLVM compiler-rt; designed to test small and fast functions via LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput.
claim_text: The libFuzzer implementation is fast but poses several restrictions on the test target (qualitative, no numbers).
found_in: book: Learn LLVM 17, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 10, Finding bugs with libFuzzer / Limitations and alternatives

name: AFL (american fuzzy lop)
listed_description: Best-known alternative fuzzer to libFuzzer; needs an instrumented binary (LLVM plugin provided) and takes input as a file path; shares corpus and dictionary format with libFuzzer. Repository is archived (Mar 2024).
found_in: book: Learn LLVM 17, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 10, Limitations and alternatives

name: LLVM ORC LLJIT
listed_description: Layered On-Request Compilation JIT engine in LLVM with compile, link, lazy and transform layers; LLJIT is the ready-made JIT stack that replaces MCJIT.
claim_text: With a JIT compiler for byte code there is no performance penalty compared to an AOT compiler (qualitative, no numbers).
found_in: book: Learn LLVM 17, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 9, LLVM's overall JIT implementation and use cases

name: LLVM XRay
listed_description: Function entry/exit instrumentation pass plus compiler-rt runtime and llvm-xray tool for call counts, accumulated times, stack reconstruction and flame graphs.
book_benchmark: Toy demo with usleep() calls only; no overhead measurement.
found_in: book: Learn LLVM 17, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 10, Performance profiling with XRay

name: LLVM new pass manager function-at-a-time pipelining
listed_description: Pass manager runs consecutive function passes on one function before the next, and shares and frees analysis results early, to improve cache behavior and avoid needless precomputation.
claim_text: Idea is to improve cache behavior: transformations touch a limited set of data (one IR function) before moving on (qualitative, no numbers).
found_in: book: Learn LLVM 17, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 7, The LLVM pass manager
